teile.einleitung: The Amazon is a huge river in South America. No other river in the world carries so much water. Around it grows the largest rainforest on Earth.
wichtigste: The Amazon flows through **South America**, mainly through Peru and Brazil.
It flows into the **Atlantic Ocean**.
It is the river with the **most water** in the world.
About 60 per cent of the Amazon rainforest lies in **Brazil**.
The pink **Amazon river dolphin** lives in the river.
The **giant water lily** has leaves that grow up to about three metres wide.

abschnitte.text: The Amazon rises in the **Andes** in Peru. From there it flows right across South America to the east. On the coast of Brazil it flows into the **Atlantic Ocean**. It is over 6,000 kilometres long. No other river carries as much **water** into the sea as the Amazon. Many large tributaries feed it.

Around the Amazon grows the largest **rainforest** on Earth. About **60 per cent** of it lies in **Brazil**. The rest is spread across several neighbouring countries such as Peru and Colombia. In the rainforest it is warm and damp all year round. An incredible number of different animals and plants live here.

**River dolphins** live in the Amazon. The **Amazon river dolphin** often turns **pink** with age. That is why it is also called the pink river dolphin. It finds its prey in the murky water with the help of clicking sounds. Many fish also live in the river, for example piranhas.

A special plant in the Amazon region is the **giant water lily**. Its round leaves float on the water. They can grow up to about **three metres** wide. The edge of the leaves is bent upwards like a baking tin. The leaves are so strong that they can carry a small child.

gewusst: When the water is high, the Amazon floods huge areas of forest every year.
Experts do not agree on whether the Amazon or the Nile is the longest river in the world.

teile.einleitung: The apoplast is a term from plant science. It describes everything in a plant that lies outside the living cell contents: the cell walls, the spaces between the cells and the dead conducting tubes. It plays a big role in the transport of water and substances.
wichtigste: The apoplast includes cell walls, intercellular spaces and dead conducting elements of the xylem.
It lies outside the plasma membranes, that is, outside the living protoplasts.
Water can flow in the apoplast without crossing a membrane.
Because there are no membranes in the way, the flow resistance is low.
The cuticle protects the apoplast of the leaves from evaporation.
The liquid in the apoplast is usually slightly acidic, around pH 5 to 6.

abschnitte.text: Every plant cell has a living part inside, the **protoplast**, which is wrapped in the **plasma membrane**. Everything outside these membranes together forms the **apoplast**. This includes the **cell walls**, the air- or water-filled **intercellular spaces** and the dead cells of the **xylem**. The counterpart is called the **symplast**: this is all the living cell contents together, which are connected with each other by fine channels, the **plasmodesmata**.

Water from the soil has to get through the root cortex to the vascular bundles. On the **apoplastic path** it flows through the network of cell walls and spaces. On the **symplastic path** it travels from cell to cell through the plasmodesmata. On the **transcellular path** it crosses every cell and its membranes, often through water channels called **aquaporins**. Because the apoplast contains no membranes, water flows there particularly easily and quickly.

The **xylem** carries water from the roots up to the leaves. Its conducting elements, the **tracheae** and **tracheids**, die as they mature. All that is left are the woody, firm cell walls, which act like tubes. Since they no longer have any living contents, they belong entirely to the apoplast. This creates a continuous conducting system outside the living cells.

In the leaves, too, the cell walls are soaked with water. So that this water does not simply evaporate, the **cuticle** lies on the outer wall of the **epidermis**. It is a waxy layer that lets almost no water through. The plant regulates gas exchange instead through small openings, the **stomata**.

abschnitte.titel: An acidic space and sugar transport
abschnitte.text: In the plasma membrane sit **proton pumps**, which move hydrogen ions (H+) outwards. That is why the liquid in the apoplast is usually slightly acidic, with a pH of around 5 to 6. The plant uses this gradient as a source of energy. In **apoplastic phloem loading**, sugar (**sucrose**) is first released into the cell wall. A **sucrose-proton symporter** then takes it up together with protons into the cells of the phloem, even against the concentration gradient.

gewusst: In the root there is a barrier: the **Casparian strip** in the endodermis seals the cell walls, so that water has to pass through living cells there.
The terms apoplast and symplast were coined around 1930 by the German forestry scientist Ernst Münch.

teile.einleitung: A floodplain is the landscape along a river that is flooded again and again. Gravel banks, pools and woods alternate here. Floodplains are among the habitats richest in species in Switzerland, but have become rare.
wichtigste: A floodplain is the area along a river that is flooded regularly.
The often flooded softwood floodplain is characterised by willows and poplars.
In the less often flooded hardwood floodplain, oaks, ashes and elms grow.
The beaver dams streams and creates new habitats.
Floodplains hold back water during floods like a sponge.
Many floodplains have disappeared because rivers were straightened and embanked.

abschnitte.text: A **floodplain** lies along a river or stream. During a flood the water overflows the banks and floods the land. In the process, gravel, sand and mud are moved around. In this way new **gravel banks**, **pools** and side channels form again and again. A floodplain is constantly changing, and that is just what makes it so valuable.

Close to the water, where flooding is frequent, lies the **softwood floodplain**. Here **willows** and **poplars** grow. They have soft wood, grow fast and withstand long floods. Further away and a little higher lies the **hardwood floodplain**. It is **flooded less often**, and **oaks**, **ashes** and **elms** with hard wood grow there.

The **beaver** is a real master builder of the floodplain. It fells trees and **dams streams**. This creates new ponds and wetlands, from which many other animals benefit. On open **gravel banks** the **little ringed plover** breeds, a small wading bird. Its eggs are so well camouflaged that they look like pebbles.

During floods, floodplains are very useful. They **hold back water like a sponge** and release it only slowly. As a result the flood peak is smaller further downstream. Water also seeps into the ground and tops up the **groundwater**. Floodplains thus also protect villages and towns.

In the past there were many more floodplains in Switzerland. Many have disappeared because **rivers were straightened and embanked** in order to gain land and to protect against floods. A well-known floodplain and forest area is the **Pfynwald** on the **Rhone in the Valais**. Today many rivers are being restored again and given more room. In this way new floodplains can form.

gewusst: Willow twigs that break off in a flood can simply take root in a new place and keep growing.
The eggs of the little ringed plover lie directly on the gravel, with no nest.

teile.einleitung: The apple tree is one of the most important fruit trees in the world and is also very common in Switzerland. In spring it bears white to pink blossoms, and in autumn crisp apples. People make sweet cider, apple purée and much more from its fruit.
wichtigste: The cultivated apple belongs to the rose family.
Its origin lies in Central Asia, mainly in Kazakhstan.
Here the apple tree blossoms in spring.
Apple blossoms are white to pink and are pollinated by bees.
There are thousands of apple varieties worldwide.
In Switzerland, freshly pressed apple juice is called Süssmost (sweet cider).
The core is often called Bütschgi in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The **cultivated apple** is a deciduous tree from the **rose family**. Standing alone, it can grow to about 8 to 15 metres tall, but in orchards it is kept small. Its leaves are egg-shaped with a serrated edge. In spring the white to pink blossoms open, and they smell sweet.

The ancestors of our apples come from the mountain forests of **Central Asia**, especially Kazakhstan. The wild apple Malus sieversii still grows there today. Apples reached Europe along the Silk Road, and the Romans spread their cultivation. The city of Almaty in Kazakhstan used to be called Alma-Ata, which is often translated as father of apples.

For an apple to form, the blossom must be **pollinated**, usually by bees. Most varieties need pollen from another apple variety nearby for this. After pollination, the apple grows from the ovary over the summer. In the middle lies the core with the pips, which in Switzerland is often called the **Bütschgi**.

Worldwide there are many thousands of **apple varieties**; popular ones include Gala, Golden Delicious, Braeburn and Bramley. To keep a variety the same, it is **grafted**: a twig of the desired variety is placed on a rootstock. A pip would grow into a tree with quite different apples. Large apple trees in meadows are called **standard trees** and provide habitat for many birds and insects.

The apple is the most important type of fruit in Switzerland. Particularly many apple trees stand in Thurgau, which is therefore jokingly called **Mostindien**. **Sweet cider** is made from freshly pressed apples, and when fermented it becomes cider, also called sour cider. And in the legend of William Tell, Tell has to shoot an apple off his son’s head.

Apple trees can become ill, for example through fungi such as **apple scab**, which causes dark spots. **Fire blight** is also dangerous, a bacterial disease in which twigs look as if they were burnt. New, resistant varieties help to reduce the use of plant protection products. Old varieties are preserved in Switzerland by organisations such as ProSpecieRara.

begriffe.erklaerung: Attaching a twig of one variety onto another tree.
A large fruit tree with a tall trunk, often in meadows.
The middle part of the apple with the pips, also called Bütschgi in Switzerland.
A plant family that also includes the rose, pear, cherry and strawberry.

gewusst: If you plant an apple pip, almost never do the same apples grow as on the parent tree.
An apple is about 85 per cent water.
The apple variety Granny Smith was named after a woman in Australia who found it in the 19th century.

teile.einleitung: When you count animals or plants in an area, at first you quickly find many new species, and later fewer and fewer. A species accumulation curve shows exactly this. With it, researchers estimate whether they have already found almost all the species.
wichtigste: The curve shows the species found in relation to the collecting effort.
If it flattens out clearly, most species have probably been recorded.
If it still rises steeply at the end, many species are still missing.
With rarefaction, species numbers are compared at equal effort.
Singletons are species that were found with only one individual.
You average over many random orders of the samples.

abschnitte.text: A **species accumulation curve** shows how many species you have found in total, depending on the **collecting effort**. The effort can be the number of samples, traps or animals counted. At the beginning the curve rises steeply, because almost every sample brings new species. Later only rare species are added, and the curve becomes flatter. It is also called a **collector’s curve**.

If the **curve flattens out clearly**, most species have probably been recorded. More samples would bring little that is new. If it **still rises steeply at the end**, many species are still missing, and **more samples are needed**. But the shape of the curve depends on the **order of the samples**. That is why you average over **many random orders** and so get a smooth curve.

Two areas can only be compared fairly if the effort was equally large. Anyone who searches twice as long usually finds more species. **Rarefaction** therefore calculates how many species you would expect in both areas at **equal effort**. In this way you compare, for example, 100 animals counted here with 100 animals counted there.

Rare species reveal how much is still missing. **Singletons** are species that were found with **one individual** only, **doubletons** those with two. The estimator **Chao1** calculates: species found plus F1² divided by 2 times F2. Here F1 is the number of singletons and F2 the number of doubletons. An example: 30 species, 8 singletons and 4 doubletons give 30 plus 64 divided by 8, that is **38 species**.

The **species-area relationship** is similar. It describes the fact that more species live in larger areas. The formula is **S = c times A to the power of z**. Here S is the number of species, A the area, and c and z are numbers that depend on the region. This relationship applies, for example, to islands of different sizes.

gewusst: With insects in tropical forests, the curve often does not flatten out even after huge effort, because there are so many rare species there.
The estimator Chao1 is named after the statistician Anne Chao.

teile.einleitung: The asteroid belt is a huge zone in the solar system in which countless chunks of rock orbit the Sun. It lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter. The chunks are leftovers from the time when the planets formed.
wichtigste: The asteroid belt lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.
Hundreds of thousands of known asteroids orbit the Sun there.
The largest body in the belt is the dwarf planet Ceres.
All the asteroids together have only a small fraction of the mass of our Moon.
The distances between asteroids are usually huge.
Jupiter’s gravity prevented a planet from forming here.
Many meteorites on Earth come from the asteroid belt.

abschnitte.text: The **asteroid belt** is a wide ring around the Sun in which very many **asteroids** orbit. Asteroids are chunks of rock and metal that are much smaller than planets. The belt lies between the orbits of **Mars** and **Jupiter**, about two to three and a half times as far from the Sun as the Earth. An asteroid usually takes three to six years to go once round the Sun.

About 4.6 billion years ago, the planets formed from dust and rock. In the region of today’s belt, the strong **gravity** of giant Jupiter disturbed this growing together. That is why no planet formed here, and many small chunks were left over. Asteroids are therefore like time capsules from the early days of the solar system.

The largest body in the belt is **Ceres**, almost 1,000 kilometres across. Giuseppe Piazzi discovered it on 1 January 1801, and since 2006 it has counted as a **dwarf planet**. The second largest is Vesta, over 500 kilometres across. Ceres alone contains a large part of the mass of the whole belt.

The NASA probe **Dawn** orbited the asteroid Vesta in 2011 and the dwarf planet Ceres from 2015. On Ceres it discovered bright spots of salt, which surprised the experts. Other probes have brought samples of asteroids to Earth. These samples help us to understand what the planets were made from.

In films, spaceships often fly through a dense swarm of rocks. In reality there are usually hundreds of thousands of kilometres between two asteroids. Space probes have therefore been able to cross the belt without any problem. If you stuck all the asteroids together, the ball would be smaller than our Moon.

When asteroids collide, smaller fragments are produced. Some of them end up on a path towards the Earth and fall down as **meteorites**. Most meteorites in museums come from the asteroid belt. Meteorites have also been found in Switzerland, for example in the area around Twannberg in the Bernese Jura.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small body of rock or metal that orbits the Sun.
A round body that is smaller than a planet and has not cleared its orbit.
A piece from space that has landed on Earth.
The path on which one body in space circles another.

gewusst: The dwarf planet Ceres was counted as a planet for almost 50 years.
The total mass of the asteroid belt is only a few per cent of the mass of the Moon.

teile.einleitung: Atropine is a strong plant poison. It occurs in deadly nightshade and in other nightshade plants. But in small, carefully measured amounts it is also an important medicine.
wichtigste: Atropine is named after deadly nightshade, whose scientific name is Atropa belladonna.
It belongs to the tropane alkaloids.
Deadly nightshade belongs to the nightshade family.
Atropine blocks the messenger substance acetylcholine.
A typical sign of poisoning is a dry mouth.
Atropine makes the heart beat faster.
In medicine it is used as an antidote for poisoning with nerve agents.

abschnitte.text: **Deadly nightshade** (Atropa belladonna) also grows in Swiss forests, often in forest clearings. It belongs to the **nightshade family**, like the potato and tomato. Its shiny black berries look harmless, but are **very poisonous**. Even a few berries can be life-threatening for children. The poison **atropine** is named after it.

The genus name **Atropa** comes from **Atropos**, one of the three **goddesses of fate** in Greek mythology. According to the legend, she cut the thread of life of human beings. The second name **belladonna** is Italian and means “beautiful woman”. In the past, women would drip the juice into their eyes to make their pupils large. This was thought beautiful at the time, but it was dangerous.

Atropine belongs to the **tropane alkaloids**. In the nervous system it blocks the messenger substance **acetylcholine**. This messenger substance controls many processes that we do not steer consciously, for example saliva and the heartbeat. When it is blocked, the result is a **dry mouth**, the **pupils become wide**, and the **heart beats faster**. In poisoning, confusion and fever are added, and you need medical help immediately.

In a carefully measured amount, atropine is a **medicine**. Eye doctors use related drugs to widen the pupil for an examination. When the heartbeat is too slow, atropine can make the heart beat faster again. It is especially important as an **antidote for poisoning with nerve agents**, for example with certain plant protection products. There it partly cancels out the dangerous effect of these substances.

Atropine does not occur only in deadly nightshade. **Thorn apple** also contains it, a plant with large white trumpet-shaped flowers and spiny fruits. It is also found in **henbane** and in angel’s trumpet. All these plants are poisonous. You should not touch them, and should wash your hands after contact.

gewusst: The berries of deadly nightshade taste slightly sweet, which makes them especially dangerous for children.
Some animals such as rabbits tolerate deadly nightshade much better than humans.

teile.einleitung: The Asian longhorned beetle is a large black beetle with white spots. It comes from China and Korea and was brought to Europe with packing wood. Its larvae eat their way through the wood of healthy broadleaved trees.
wichtigste: The beetle originally comes from China and Korea.
It was brought to Europe mainly with packing wood such as pallets.
The larvae damage the wood of trunk and branches.
In Europe it attacks maples particularly often.
Adult beetles are shiny black with white spots and very long antennae.
In Switzerland, infested trees are felled and destroyed.

abschnitte.text: The **Asian longhorned beetle** (Anoplophora glabripennis) belongs to the **longhorn beetles**. The adult beetle is **shiny black** with **white spots**. It grows to about 2 to 4 centimetres long. Striking are the **very long antennae**, which are ringed in black and white. They can be longer than the whole body.

The beetle originally lives in **China and Korea**. It came to Europe and North America mainly with **packing wood**, for example with **pallets** and crates. The larvae hid in them. To prevent this, there is the international standard **ISPM 15**. It requires, for example, that packing wood be heated **in its core to at least 56 degrees Celsius for 30 minutes**. Treated wood carries a special mark.

The **larvae** eat their way through the **wood of trunk and branches**. This creates long tunnels, which weaken the tree. Branches can break off, and whole trees can die. Unlike many other beetles, it also attacks **healthy trees**. In Europe it hits **maple** particularly often, but also poplars, willows, birches and other broadleaved trees.

An infestation shows itself in **perfectly round exit holes** about **1 centimetre across**. The finished beetles leave the tree through them. At the foot of the trunk or in forks of branches you often find **boring dust**. You can also see funnel-shaped places in the bark where the female laid her eggs. Anyone who notices something like this should report it to the authorities.

In Switzerland the beetle counts as a **particularly dangerous harmful organism**, and a find must be reported. Since 2011, several infestation sites have been discovered. **Infested trees are felled and destroyed**, usually by chipping and burning. Around the site, the trees are checked for several years, partly with specially trained **sniffer dogs**. In this way some infestation sites have been wiped out again.

gewusst: Sniffer dogs can smell the scent of the larvae and the boring dust in wood.
Development from larva to finished beetle usually takes one to two years.

teile.einleitung: Ammonification is an important step in the nitrogen cycle. In it, bacteria and fungi break down dead organisms and waste and release the nitrogen bound in them as ammonium. This makes the nitrogen available to plants again.
wichtigste: In **ammonification**, nitrogen bound in organic matter is released as **ammonium**.
It is carried out mainly by **bacteria and fungi**.
The nitrogen comes from **proteins**, **nucleic acids** and **urea**.
The enzyme **urease** splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide.
Ammonification takes place with and without oxygen.
In well-aerated soils it is usually followed by **nitrification**.

abschnitte.text: When plants and animals die, their organic matter is left behind. **Decomposers** such as bacteria and fungi break it down. In doing so they split **proteins** into amino acids and release **ammonium** (NH₄⁺) or **ammonia** (NH₃) from them. This process is called **ammonification**. It is a central part of the **nitrogen cycle**.

In living things, nitrogen is bound mainly in **amino acids** and proteins. **Nucleic acids**, the building blocks of genetic material, also contain nitrogen. Added to this are waste products such as **urea**. Cellulose, starch and fats, on the other hand, contain no nitrogen. In ammonification, only the nitrogen from the nitrogen-containing substances is released.

abschnitte.titel: Urease and the smell of slurry
abschnitte.text: The enzyme **urease** is found in many bacteria. It splits urea very quickly into **ammonia** and carbon dioxide. That is why ammonia quickly forms in stables and **slurry pits**. The gas escapes and causes the sharp smell of stored slurry. Ammonium and ammonia are in **equilibrium**: at a high, alkaline pH there is more volatile ammonia, which can be lost as a gas.

A great many different microorganisms can release ammonium. Ammonification therefore takes place **aerobically** (with oxygen) and **anaerobically** (without oxygen). It even happens in wet, oxygen-poor soils. In well **aerated** soils, the ammonium is then quickly oxidised by **nitrification** to nitrite and nitrate. This completes the path from dead biomass to plant nutrient.

gewusst: Ammonia losses from slurry are an environmental issue in Switzerland, because ammonia can over-fertilise sensitive forests and moors.
Trailing hoses put slurry directly onto the soil, so less ammonia escapes.

teile.einleitung: An old-wood island is a small patch of forest where the trees are left to grow old and decay on their own. No timber is cut there. This creates a habitat for many animals, fungi and plants that depend on old and dead wood.
wichtigste: In an **old-wood island** the trees stay standing until they decay naturally.
Individual valuable trees with holes or fungi are called **habitat trees**.
Living things that depend on wood are called **xylobionts**.
Old-wood islands act as **stepping stones** between larger reserves.
The rare **white-backed woodpecker** needs deciduous forests rich in dead wood.
Old-wood islands are usually smaller than natural forest reserves and are often protected only for a set period.

abschnitte.text: In a managed forest, trees are usually felled long before they are old. A lot of habitat is lost this way. In an **old-wood island**, no timber is harvested. The trees are allowed to grow old, die and decay. This produces a lot of **dead wood**. Old-wood islands are complemented by individual **habitat trees**, also called biotope trees. These are trees with woodpecker holes, cracks or fungi, which are left standing because of their value to nature.

Dead wood is anything but dead. Many living things depend on it. They are called **xylobionts**, which means wood dwellers. They include numerous **beetles**, fungi and lichens. They break the wood down or live in holes and crevices. The **tinder fungus**, for example, grows on weakened and dead beech trees and forms large, bracket-shaped fruiting bodies. It breaks the wood down as **white rot**.

A particularly demanding resident is the **white-backed woodpecker**. This rare woodpecker looks for insect larvae mainly in rotting deciduous wood. It only occurs where there is a lot of dead wood. An overview by Müller and Bütler (2010) showed that many demanding dead-wood species need around **20 to 50 cubic metres** of dead wood per hectare, depending on the type of forest.

Many dead-wood species can only spread over short distances. That is why a **network** of protected areas is important. **Natural forest reserves** are large and secured for the long term. **Old-wood islands** are smaller and in Switzerland are often protected for a certain period through contracts. They act as **stepping stones** between the reserves. This allows animals and fungi to move from one area to the next.

gewusst: In the past, people used the tinder fungus to light fires, which is how it got its name.
In a natural forest with no timber harvesting, a tree can live for several hundred years before it decays.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss pine nut is the seed of the Swiss stone pine, a conifer of the Alps. Unlike many other conifers, the Swiss stone pine does not let the wind spread its seeds. Animals take care of that, above all a bird, the spotted nutcracker.
wichtigste: The Swiss pine nut is the seed of the Swiss stone pine, also called the Arolla pine.
Swiss stone pine seeds have no wing.
A ripe cone does not open by itself, animals break it open.
A Swiss stone pine cone needs about two years to ripen.
Young cones are violet.
A Swiss pine nut is about 1 centimetre in size.

abschnitte.titel: The Swiss stone pine, a tree of the mountains
abschnitte.text: The **Swiss stone pine** (Pinus cembra) is also called the **Arolla pine** or Zirbe. It grows in the Alps up to the **tree line** and withstands great cold. Its needles stand in bundles of five. In Switzerland it is common, for example, in the **Engadine** and in the Valais. Swiss stone pines can live for several hundred years.

**Young cones** are **violet**, and later they turn brown. A cone needs **about two years** to ripen. Inside are the **Swiss pine nuts**, which are about **1 centimetre** in size. The seeds of the Swiss stone pine lack **a wing**, of the kind that the seeds of the spruce, for example, have. That is why the wind cannot carry them far.

A ripe cone **does not open by itself**. **Animals break it open** to get at the nuts. The most important helper is the **spotted nutcracker**, a member of the crow family. In autumn it gathers many nuts and hides them in the ground as a winter store. It finds many of its hiding places again, even under snow. New Swiss stone pines grow from the forgotten nuts.

The **red squirrel** also likes to eat Swiss pine nuts. Mice and other animals take their share as well. The nuts are rich in fat and are therefore valuable winter food. People eat Swiss pine nuts too. In the Grisons they are used, for example, for pastries and sweets.

gewusst: A single spotted nutcracker can hide many thousands of Swiss pine nuts in one autumn.
Swiss stone pine wood has a strong scent and is often used for parlours, furniture and beds.

teile.einleitung: Artemisinin is an active substance from sweet wormwood. It works against malaria, a dangerous disease in warm countries. Its discoverer, Tu Youyou, received the Nobel Prize for it in 2015.
wichtigste: Artemisinin is obtained from sweet wormwood.
It is used mainly against malaria.
Tu Youyou received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2015 for the discovery.
What mattered was an extract made at a low temperature instead of boiling.
An endoperoxide bridge in the molecule is important for its effect.
Artemisinin is given together with a second active substance to prevent resistance.

abschnitte.text: **Sweet wormwood** (Artemisia annua) is a plant from the daisy family. In **traditional Chinese medicine** it has been used against fever for a very long time. The active substance **artemisinin** is obtained from its leaves. Chemically it belongs to the **sesquiterpene lactones**, a group of natural substances.

**Malaria** is caused by tiny single-celled organisms, the **plasmodia**. They are passed on by the bite of certain mosquitoes, the **Anopheles mosquitoes**. The disease causes high fever and can be fatal without treatment. Children in Africa south of the Sahara are especially affected. Against older drugs such as chloroquine, many of the parasites became **resistant** over time, that is, insensitive.

The Chinese researcher **Tu Youyou** searched old writings in the 1960s and 1970s for remedies against malaria. The first extracts from wormwood worked badly. In an old text she found the hint to soak the plant in cold water. She then extracted the active substance **at a low temperature instead of by boiling**, and it worked. In 2015 she received the **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine** for it.

In the artemisinin molecule there is a special link of two oxygen atoms, the **endoperoxide bridge**. It is crucial for the effect. When the substance comes into contact with iron in the parasite, very reactive particles form, which damage the parasite. Artemisinin works quickly, but stays in the body only for a short time.

Artemisinin or its derivatives are almost always given together with a **second active substance**. This **combination therapy** is meant to **prevent resistance** and kill the remaining parasites. Improved substances were developed from artemisinin, for example **artemether** and **artesunate**. **Artesunate** is injected for **severe malaria**. Combination therapies are now among the most important remedies against malaria.

gewusst: Tu Youyou was the first woman from China to receive a Nobel Prize in a natural science.
The hint about soaking in cold water came from a Chinese book more than 1,600 years old.

teile.einleitung: Species diversity means how many different kinds of animals, plants, fungi and tiny living things there are. It is an important part of biodiversity. Some habitats are especially rich in species, and much has not even been discovered yet.
wichtigste: Around 2 million species have been scientifically described worldwide.
Insects make up most of the known animal species.
The tropical rainforest is regarded as the habitat richest in species on land.
Coral reefs are called the “rainforest of the seas”.
From the poles to the equator, species diversity increases.
In Switzerland, dry meadows are among the habitats richest in species.
Invasive species can push out native species.

abschnitte.text: **Biodiversity** includes three levels: the diversity of **habitats**, the diversity of **species** and the **genetic diversity** within a species. **Species diversity** counts how many different species there are. Around **2 million species** have been scientifically described worldwide. But experts suspect that there are many more that nobody knows. Every year thousands of new species are discovered.

**Insects** make up most of the known animal species. Of the **beetles** alone, several hundred thousand species are known. Add to that butterflies, flies, ants, bees and many more. Mammals, by comparison, are a small group with a few thousand species. Many insects are tiny and live hidden, so many are still unknown.

abschnitte.titel: Where there are especially many species
abschnitte.text: From the **poles towards the equator, species diversity increases**. On land, the **tropical rainforest** is the habitat richest in species. On a single tree there, hundreds of insect species can live. In the sea, **coral reefs** are especially rich in life. That is why they are often called the **“rainforest of the seas”**.

Thanks to mountains, valleys, lakes and rivers, Switzerland too has many habitats. **Dry meadows** and **dry pastures** are especially rich in species. Many flowers grow on them, and many butterflies, grasshoppers and wild bees live there. Such meadows are low in nutrients and are fertilised very little. Many of them have disappeared because the land was fertilised, built on or no longer mown.

Some species are brought by humans into new areas. If they spread strongly and **push out native species**, they are called **invasive species**. An example in Switzerland is the **Canadian goldenrod** from North America. It blooms **golden yellow** and often grows on **railway embankments**, at the edges of paths and on waste ground. Where it forms dense stands, other plants have hardly any room left.

gewusst: Many experts estimate that there are several million still unknown species on Earth.
A single gram of soil can contain millions of bacteria from thousands of species.

teile.einleitung: An anthill is the home of an entire ant colony. The large mounds in the forest are built by red wood ants from needles, twigs and soil. In Switzerland these ants are protected.
wichtigste: The large mounds in the forest are built by **red wood ants**.
The **queen** lays the eggs, and the workers look after the brood.
Wood ants have been **protected** in Switzerland since 1966.
To defend themselves they spray **formic acid**.
They collect sweet **honeydew** from aphids.
A large colony can have many hundreds of thousands of ants.

abschnitte.text: **Red wood ants** build mounds that can grow to more than a metre high. To do this they gather needles, small twigs and pieces of plants. The nest also reaches deep into the ground. They prefer to build in **sunny spots**, such as at the edges of forests or in clearings. The ants need warmth for their brood.

Very many ants live together in an anthill, in a large colony **many hundreds of thousands**. The **queen** lays the eggs from which the colony grows. With wood ants there are often several queens in one nest. The many **workers** look after the brood, build the mound and fetch food. They all work together like one big team.

If an anthill is disturbed, the ants spray **formic acid**. It stings and drives enemies away. Ants also have a special friendship with **aphids**. The aphids give off a sugary juice, the **honeydew**. The ants drink it and in return protect the aphids from enemies.

Wood ants are very useful to the forest. One colony catches a great many **insects**, including pests that weaken trees. That is why they are called the **health police of the forest**. In Switzerland, red wood ants have been **protected since 1966**. Their nests must not be damaged. If you see an anthill, it is best to look at it from a little distance and leave it untouched.

gewusst: Ants find their way using scent trails that they leave on the ground.
An anthill works like a heater: in spring it is often much warmer inside than outside.

teile.einleitung: ATP synthase is a tiny protein motor in the membranes of cells. It makes ATP, the most important energy carrier of all living things. It is driven by a flow of protons.
wichtigste: ATP synthase forms ATP with the help of a proton gradient.
Peter Mitchell explained this with the chemiosmotic theory and received the Nobel Prize in 1978.
In chloroplasts, the protons flow from the thylakoid lumen into the stroma.
One part of the enzyme turns like a rotor.
The formation of ATP using light energy is called photophosphorylation.
Uncouplers stop the formation of ATP.

abschnitte.text: **ATP** stands for adenosine triphosphate. It is the energy currency of the cell: almost all processes that need energy use ATP. **ATP synthase** puts ATP together from ADP and phosphate. It sits in the membranes of the **mitochondria** and of the **chloroplasts** of plants. In chloroplasts its formation with the help of light is called **photophosphorylation**, in mitochondria **oxidative phosphorylation**.

In chloroplasts, ATP synthase consists of two main parts. **CF0** is embedded in the membrane and lets the protons through. **CF1** projects into the stroma and forms the ATP there. The C stands for chloroplast. The flow of protons sets a ring in the membrane and the **gamma subunit** attached to it turning. This **rotor** changes the shape of the centres in the head part, where ATP is made.

abschnitte.titel: Protons like water at a dam
abschnitte.text: In photosynthesis, the electron transport chain pumps protons into the inner space of the thylakoids, the **thylakoid lumen**. There their concentration is high. Following the gradient, the protons flow back through ATP synthase into the **stroma**. This is like water flowing through a turbine. Substances that make the membrane permeable to protons are called **uncouplers**. Then electron transport carries on, but ATP synthase no longer gets any drive.

**Peter Mitchell** was the first to explain that a **proton gradient** across a membrane drives the formation of ATP. For this **chemiosmotic theory** he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in **1978**. **André Jagendorf** confirmed it in 1966: in the dark he moved chloroplasts from an acidic to a basic solution, and they made ATP without light. **Paul Boyer** and **John Walker** worked out exactly how the enzyme works. For this they received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in **1997**.

gewusst: ATP synthase is one of the smallest rotary motors known in nature.
Every day a person builds up and breaks down about as much ATP as they weigh themselves.

teile.einleitung: The pineapple is a sweet, juicy fruit from warm countries. It originally comes from South America. With its scaly skin and its green crown of leaves, it looks very special.
wichtigste: The pineapple comes from **South America**.
It is a **multiple fruit** made of many berries grown together.
It takes **more than a year** before a plant bears a fruit.
A new plant can grow from the **crown of leaves**.
Fresh pineapple contains **bromelain**, which breaks down protein.
In German it is called **“Ananas”**, in English **“pineapple”**.

abschnitte.text: The pineapple comes from **South America**. The people there had been growing it for a long time. **Christopher Columbus** got to know it on his travels and brought news of it to Europe. Later it was planted in many warm countries. In the 20th century, **Hawaii** was famous for its huge pineapple fields. Today most pineapple is grown in other countries.

A pineapple is not really a single fruit. It is a **multiple fruit**. Many small flowers produce berries that **grow together** into one large fruit. The scales on the skin show where the individual flowers sat. Each plant usually produces only one large fruit at a time, and it takes **more than a year** for it to ripen.

Fresh pineapple sometimes tingles on the tongue. This is because of a substance called **bromelain**. It breaks down **protein** and can therefore irritate the tongue. In tinned pineapple, the substance is usually inactive because of the heating. That is why it does not tingle.

You can do an experiment with the **crown of leaves** of a pineapple. You twist it off and let it dry out a little. Then you put it in soil. The crown can grow **roots**, and a new pineapple plant grows. But it needs plenty of warmth, light and patience before it bears a fruit.

gewusst: The German word “Ananas” and the English word “pineapple” both describe the same fruit. “Pineapple” originally meant pine cone, because the fruit reminded people of one.
The pineapple belongs to the bromeliad family. Many of its relatives grow on trees in the rainforest.

teile.einleitung: Stoneworts are green algae that grow on the bed of clear lakes and ponds. With their whorled side branches they look like little candelabras. They are regarded as a sign of clean water.
wichtigste: Stoneworts owe their German name, “Armleuchteralgen”, which means candelabra algae, to their whorled side branches.
Important genera are Chara and Nitella.
The shoot is divided into nodes and long internodes.
They are anchored in the bed with thread-like rhizoids.
Many Chara species deposit lime and feel rough.
If they return to a lake, the water quality has improved.

abschnitte.text: Stoneworts are **green algae**. On their shoot the side branches stand in **whorls**, that is, in a circle at the same height. This is reminiscent of a **candelabra** with many arms. Well-known genera are **Chara** and **Nitella**. Stoneworts are close relatives of land plants and often grow up to half a metre long or longer.

The shoot is divided into **nodes** and long sections in between, the **internodes**. The side branches grow at the nodes. The algae have no roots. They are anchored in the bed with thread-like **rhizoids**. Many species of the genus **Chara** deposit **lime** on their surface. That is why they feel **rough and brittle**.

The internodes often consist of a single, very long cell that can reach several centimetres. In these **giant cells** you can see well under the microscope how the inside of the cell moves. This movement is called **cytoplasmic streaming**. Researchers also study **electrical signals** that travel through the cell in stoneworts. In this way the algae help us to understand processes in plant cells in general.

Most stoneworts need **clear, nutrient-poor water**. If a lake is over-fertilised, the water becomes cloudy with algal blooms, and the stoneworts disappear. If they return later, this shows an **improvement in water quality**. Dense stands are very useful for a lake: they **bind nutrients**, **stabilise the sediment** and **keep the water clear**. They also give fish and small animals shelter and food.

gewusst: In some lakes, stoneworts form real underwater meadows on the bottom.
The lime that stoneworts deposit can build up on the lake bed over a long time and contribute to so-called lake marl.

teile.einleitung: The Angiosperm Phylogeny Group, or APG for short, is an international team of researchers. It arranges all flowering plants in a shared system based on comparisons of DNA. This system has greatly changed the study of plants.
wichtigste: APG stands for **Angiosperm Phylogeny Group**.
The first version of the system appeared in **1998**.
The version **APG IV** appeared in **2016** and recognises 64 orders and 416 families.
The system is based on **comparisons of DNA sequences**.
It only accepts **monophyletic groups**.
**Amborella trichopoda** is regarded as the sister group of all other flowering plants.

abschnitte.text: In the past, plants were arranged mainly by their **shape**, for example by flowers and leaves. But plants that look similar are not always closely related. The **APG** therefore arranges the families according to **molecular analyses of relationships**, that is, by comparing DNA sequences. The first version, **APG I**, appeared in **1998**. It was followed by APG II (2003), APG III (2009) and **APG IV (2016)**. It was the first widely supported system based on DNA.

The APG system only accepts **monophyletic** groups. Such a group includes one ancestor and **all** of its descendants. That is why old groups were dropped, for example the **dicotyledons** in the old sense. The version APG IV appeared in the Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society. It recognises **64 orders** and **416 families**.

abschnitte.titel: The root of the family tree
abschnitte.text: Right at the base of the flowering plants stands **Amborella trichopoda**, a shrub from **New Caledonia**. It is the only species in its order. Its line split off first from all other flowering plants. After that, the **Nymphaeales**, which include the water lilies, and the **Austrobaileyales** branch off. Together with the Amborellales they form the so-called **“ANA grade”**.

Many well-known plants belong to two large groups: the **rosids** and the **asterids**. The **pea** belongs to the Fabales, an order of the rosids. The **sunflower** belongs to the Asterales, the **potato** to the Solanales. Both orders count as asterids. Tomato, lavender and coffee are also asterids.

gewusst: Water lilies belong to the oldest lines of flowering plants.
Many identification guides and botanical gardens have rearranged their order according to the APG system.

teile.einleitung: A brushwood pile looks unremarkable, but it is a valuable habitat. Between the piled-up branches, many animals find shelter, food and a place to spend the winter. That is why nature conservationists encourage brushwood piles in gardens, at the edges of forests and in farming.
wichtigste: A brushwood pile consists of piled-up branches and twigs.
Hedgehogs like to hibernate in brushwood piles.
You should not simply set fire to a brushwood pile, because animals may be sleeping in it.
The wren likes to build its nest in dense brushwood.
The slow worm likes to hide under brushwood piles.
Fungi and insects break down the wood over the years.

abschnitte.titel: More than a pile of wood
abschnitte.text: A **brushwood pile** consists of **piled-up branches and twigs**, of the kind that arise when hedges and trees are cut. Between the branches many **hollow spaces** form. There it is sheltered, a little warmer in winter and shady in summer. A good pile is one that is big enough and may stay for a long time. At the bottom you can lay thicker branches, and at the top finer twigs.

The **hedgehog** likes to use brushwood piles as a refuge and **hibernates** in them. The **slow worm**, a legless lizard, likes to hide under the branches. Lizards, toads, mice and many beetles also find shelter here. The **wren** is a small brown bird with a **cocked tail**. It likes to build its nest in **dense brushwood**.

In time the wood becomes rotten. **Fungi and insects** break it down over the years. This produces valuable soil. Many beetle larvae and wild bees live in dead wood. To keep the habitat going, new branches are laid on top again and again.

In farming, brushwood piles are made specially for **weasels**, for example for the stoat. Weasels hunt mice and need safe hiding places along hedges and field edges. Often the brushwood pile is combined with a **nesting chamber made of wood**. It is a **protected place for the young**. Several such piles in a row help the weasels to move safely through the landscape.

abschnitte.titel: Do not simply set it alight
abschnitte.text: Sometimes brushwood piles are burnt, for example for a fire on 1 August. This is dangerous for animals, because **hedgehogs and other animals can sleep in them**. It is better to pile up the wood for a fire only shortly beforehand. An old brushwood pile should be moved over before it is lit. A related idea is the **Benjes hedge**: it is made of **loosely piled branches**, in which shrubs sprout in time.

gewusst: The Benjes hedge is named after the German landscape gardener Hermann Benjes.
Birds carry seeds into a Benjes hedge, and new shrubs grow from these seeds in time.

teile.einleitung: A floodplain forest grows along rivers and is flooded regularly. Such forests are wild, damp and full of life. In Switzerland they have become rare and are now protected.
wichtigste: A floodplain forest is flooded regularly by a river.
In the softwood floodplain close to the water, willows and poplars grow.
Typical of the hardwood floodplain are ash, oak and elm.
Around 90 per cent of Swiss floodplains have disappeared over time.
Today floodplains cover only about 0.5 per cent of the country’s area.
Since 1992 there has been a federal inventory of floodplains of national importance.

abschnitte.text: A **floodplain forest** grows near a river and is **flooded regularly**. The trees then stand in water for a time. The soil is often damp and rich in nutrients, which the flood brings with it. Only trees that can withstand flooding can grow here. Climbers such as **traveller’s joy** and **hop** climb up the trunks.

Close to the water lies the **softwood floodplain**. Here mainly **willows** and **poplars** grow. They are flooded often and for long periods. Further from the river and a little higher lies the **hardwood floodplain**. It is **flooded less often**. Typical tree species there are **ash**, **oak** and **elm**.

Floodplains count as especially **species-rich habitats**. The reason: **floods create new habitats again and again**. Besides the forest there are gravel banks, pools, oxbow lakes and swamps. In them live amphibians, dragonflies, fish, birds and many rare plants. Dead wood also stays where it falls and provides food for beetles and fungi.

Floodplain forests are also useful to people. They **take up water** and **slow down floods**. The water spreads over the area and flows on more slowly. The soil also filters the water and tops up the **groundwater**. Many municipalities get their drinking water from such areas.

In the past there were large floodplains along almost all Swiss rivers. Through straightening, dams, power stations and new building land, **around 90 per cent** of them have disappeared. Today floodplains cover only **about 0.5 per cent of the country’s area**. Since **1992** there has been a **federal inventory of floodplains of national importance**, which protects the most valuable areas. In addition, rivers are being restored in many places so that floodplain forests can form again.

gewusst: Although floodplains cover only a tiny part of Switzerland, a large part of all native species occur there.
The seeds of willows and poplars fly away on white hairs and like to sprout on fresh gravel.

teile.einleitung: Because of climate change, the habitats of many species are shifting. Some species cannot follow fast enough. In assisted migration, humans bring them in a targeted way to areas that will suit them in future. The idea is controversial.
wichtigste: Assisted migration is the targeted relocation of species to areas that will suit them climatically in future.
The term means a migration that is helped along.
The species is brought to places where it did not occur before.
A frequently mentioned risk: the species could become invasive in the new area.
In forestry, seed from warmer origins of the same species is used.
A well-known example is the conifer Torreya taxifolia from Florida.

abschnitte.text: **Assisted migration** means a **migration that is helped along**. It refers to the **targeted relocation** of species to areas that will **suit them climatically in future**. This is a particular issue for species with a **low ability to spread**. They cannot shift their range fast enough when the climate changes. These include many plants and small animals that only cover short distances.

In a classic **reintroduction**, a species is brought back to where it lived before. An example is the ibex in the Swiss Alps. In assisted migration, by contrast, a species is **brought to places where it did not occur before**. This is a bigger intervention in nature. That is why it is much discussed among experts.

**Torreya taxifolia** is a seriously threatened conifer from Florida. In its small natural area, many trees are dying. A **citizens’ group** therefore began planting trees **far to the north** of its previous range. Supporters see in this a chance to save the species. Critics complain that this happened without thorough scientific examination.

abschnitte.titel: In the forest of the future
abschnitte.text: In forestry there is a more cautious form, **assisted population migration**. In it, **seed from warmer origins of the same species** is used, but within its range. An example would be beeches from a drier, warmer region that are planted further north. In Switzerland, too, researchers are testing in trial plantings which tree species and origins cope with a warmer climate.

A frequently mentioned risk is that the relocated species becomes **invasive** in the new area and pushes out native species. Diseases and pests could also be brought along. Many experts therefore demand clear conditions. The species should be **seriously threatened without help**, and the **risk in the target area** should be thoroughly **examined** beforehand. Others think it is more important to link habitats so that species can migrate by themselves.

gewusst: The citizens’ group that is bringing Torreya taxifolia northwards calls itself the “Torreya Guardians”.
Even today, tree species that cope better with heat and drought than the previous ones are sometimes planted in forests.

teile.einleitung: Alpine farming means that animals are kept on high mountain pastures in summer. There the milk is often made into cheese straight away. In Switzerland, alpine farming has a tradition going back centuries, with many customs.
wichtigste: On the alp the animals eat mountain grass and **alpine herbs**.
Cheese is made in the **dairy hut**, where the alp staff often live too.
The milk is heated in a large **copper cauldron**.
Many alps belong to **alp cooperatives**, corporations or municipalities.
In the past, **alp pigs** were fed with the whey.
Customs include the **alp blessing** and the **Chästeilet** in the Justistal.

abschnitte.text: In summer, farmers take their animals up to the alp. There they graze on the natural **mountain meadows**, which are rich in herbs and flowers. This time is called **summering**. Meanwhile the grass in the valley can be mown and stored as hay for the winter. Many alps do not belong to a single farmer, but to **alp cooperatives**, corporations or municipalities. The members may summer their animals there and share the work.

abschnitte.titel: Making cheese in the dairy hut
abschnitte.text: The most important building on the alp is the **dairy hut**. In it stand the **cheese cauldron** and the cheese press. The cauldron is a large kettle, often made of **copper**, which hangs over the fire. The milk is warmed in it and curdled with **rennet**. A lot of **whey** is left over when cheese is made. In the past, **pigs** were fattened with it on many alps, so nothing was wasted.

Bells help the herdsman to find the animals on the wide pasture. One special bell is the **treichel**. It is forged from sheet metal and has a deep sound. Treichel bells are hung on cows or carried in parades. When the animals go up to the alp and come down again, you can hear their sound from far away.

On some alps the herdsman speaks or sings the **alp blessing** in the evening, also called the **Betruf**. He calls it out across the alp through a wooden milk funnel. The blessing is meant to protect animals and people during the night. It is found mainly in Catholic alpine regions. In the **Justistal** in the canton of Bern, the **Chästeilet** takes place in autumn: the summer’s cheese is shared out fairly among the farmers, according to how much milk their cows gave.

gewusst: The Chästeilet in the Justistal attracts many spectators every year.
Alpine cheese tastes a little different from alp to alp, because the cows eat different herbs everywhere.

teile.einleitung: Arnica is a bright yellow mountain flower from the daisy family. It grows on poor meadows and is known as a medicinal plant. But you must not eat it, because it is poisonous.
wichtigste: Arnica has yellow to orange flowers.
It belongs to the daisy family.
Another name is Bergwohlverleih.
The leaves on the stem grow in opposite pairs.
It flowers in summer.
Arnica ointments are used externally for bruises.
Arnica cannot stand a lot of fertiliser on the meadow.

abschnitte.text: **Arnica** (Arnica montana) has large, **yellow to orange** flower heads. As in all **members of the daisy family**, a flower head is made up of many small individual flowers. At ground level it forms a rosette of leaves. On the stem the leaves stand **in opposite pairs**. This is how you can tell it apart from similar yellow flowers.

Arnica grows on **poor meadows and pastures**, especially in the mountains. In Switzerland it is found mainly in the Jura and the Alps. It prefers rather acidic, nutrient-poor soils. It cannot stand **a lot of fertiliser** at all, because then other plants get stronger and push it out. Because such meadows have become rarer, arnica too has become rarer in many places.

Arnica **flowers in summer**, usually from June to August. Then its flowers shine far across the mountain meadows. Many insects such as bees and butterflies visit it. Later small fruits with a crown of hairs form, which the wind carries away.

abschnitte.titel: A medicinal plant for the skin
abschnitte.text: Arnica is an old **medicinal plant**. Its old name **Bergwohlverleih** shows how much good people expected of it. Ointments, gels and tinctures with arnica are used **externally**, for example for **bruises**, contusions and sprains. You should not put it on open wounds. Some people react sensitively to it on the skin.

Arnica is **poisonous** if you eat it or drink it as tea. It can cause stomach pain and heart problems. So the rule is: use it only externally, and only ready-made products from a pharmacy or chemist. In many areas wild arnica is also **protected** and must not be picked.

gewusst: For medicines, arnica is nowadays often grown in fields, so that the wild populations are spared.
The name Arnica montana means that the plant grows in the mountains: montana means “in the mountains”.

teile.einleitung: Every animal and plant species lives in a particular area, its range. When the climate warms, these areas shift: towards the poles and upwards in height. This range shift can also be observed in the Swiss Alps.
wichtigste: The range is the area where a species is found.
With warming, many ranges shift towards the poles and to greater heights.
In the mountains it gets about 0.65 °C cooler for every 100 metres of height.
On many European mountain summits, more plant species grow today than before.
The alpine tree line is slowly rising in many places.
Fragmented habitats make it harder for species to follow their climate.

abschnitte.text: The **range** is the area where a species occurs naturally. Its limits often depend on the climate, for example on how cold the winters or how dry the summers are. When it gets warmer, the suitable zone shifts. Many species then move **towards the poles**, in Europe that means north, or **to greater heights**. At the warm edge of their range, on the other hand, they can disappear.

In the mountains the temperature falls by about **0.65 °C per 100 metres of height**. If it gets 1.3 °C warmer, a certain temperature zone therefore lies about **200 metres** higher than before. Long-term observations on European **mountain summits** show that the **number of plant species is increasing** there, because species move up from below. The **tree line** is also slowly rising in many places.

For species that already live right at the top, things get tight. They are pushed higher and higher until **no habitat is left** above them. Experts therefore speak of an **“escalator to extinction”**. Affected are, for example, specialised alpine plants and animals that need cold. The smaller a mountain, the sooner the summit is reached.

How fast climate zones move across the landscape is described by **climate velocity**, for example in kilometres per year. Birds and many insects can fly and follow the climate quite quickly. **Plants** are slower: they spread only by **seeds**, from generation to generation. In addition, the **fragmentation** of habitats hinders many species. Roads, settlements and intensively farmed fields separate the areas from each other.

The forests of Switzerland are changing too. The **Norway spruce** is an important tree species, but it was often planted at low altitudes in the Central Plateau as well. There it suffers more and more from **drought** and **bark beetles**. At low altitudes it is therefore considered particularly at risk. Foresters are increasingly relying on tree species that cope better with warmth and dryness.

gewusst: One degree of warming corresponds to roughly 150 metres of height in the mountains.
On some Alpine summits the number of plant species has risen clearly in recent decades.

teile.einleitung: Ragweed is a plant from North America that has spread in Europe. Its pollen causes severe allergies in many people. That is why it is actively controlled in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Ragweed pollen is one of the **strongest allergy triggers**.
The plant comes from **North America**.
It was often brought in with contaminated **bird seed**.
In Switzerland it must be **reported and controlled by law**.
It flowers in **late summer and autumn**, roughly from August to October.
Its pollen is spread by the **wind**.

abschnitte.text: The most common species is called **common ragweed** in English. Its finely divided leaves are reminiscent of mugwort, and its small flower heads grow in spikes. The plant comes from **North America**. In Europe it spread mainly in the 20th century. Plants that spread strongly in a new area and cause problems are called **invasive**.

abschnitte.titel: Into the garden with bird seed
abschnitte.text: Ragweed seeds were often found in bird seed mixtures in the past. Under the **bird feeders** they fell to the ground and sprouted. This is how ragweed reached many gardens. Today people make sure that bird seed is free of ragweed seeds. It can also be spread through soil and construction machinery.

Ragweed is a **wind-pollinated plant** and produces huge amounts of light pollen grains. These can be carried a long way through the air. Even **very few** pollen grains per cubic metre of air can cause symptoms in sensitive people. The pollen can cause **hay fever** and **asthma**. Because ragweed flowers from August to October, it extends the pollen season into autumn for allergy sufferers.

In Switzerland, ragweed must be **reported and controlled by law**. Anyone who finds it must remove it and report the find to the authorities. This is meant to stop it from spreading. When pulling it out, you wear **gloves**, because the plant sap can irritate the skin. If the plant is already flowering, a **dust mask** protects against the pollen. It is best to pull the plants out with their roots before they flower.

gewusst: A single large ragweed plant can produce thousands of seeds, which stay able to sprout in the soil for many years.
In Greek legend, “ambrosia” was the food of the gods. The plant shares only the name with it.

teile.einleitung: Essential oils are strongly scented substances that plants make in their leaves, flowers, peels or bark. They give peppermint, lavender or lemon their typical smell. Unlike fatty oils, they evaporate easily.
wichtigste: Most essential oils are obtained by steam distillation.
Oils from citrus peel are usually cold pressed.
Essential oils evaporate and leave no lasting grease spot.
Distillation also produces scented water, the hydrolate.
Members of the mint family store their oil in glandular hairs on the leaves.
Well-known ingredients are eugenol, thymol, chamazulene and 1,8-cineole.

abschnitte.text: **Essential oils** are mixtures of many different scented substances. Plants make them, among other reasons, to deter animals that would eat them or to attract insects. In **members of the mint family** such as peppermint and sage, they sit in tiny **glandular hairs** on the leaf surface. If you rub a leaf, these burst open and the scent is released.

Although they are called oils, essential oils are not fats. They are **volatile**, which means they evaporate easily. You can test this simply: a drop of essential oil on paper **evaporates** and leaves **no lasting grease spot**. A drop of cooking oil, that is a **fatty oil**, on the other hand makes a lasting, translucent spot. Essential oils hardly dissolve in water, but dissolve well in alcohol and fat.

Most essential oils are obtained by **steam distillation**. Hot steam flows through the plant parts and takes the scented substances with it. Then the steam is cooled. The oil then floats on the water and can be separated. The scented water that is left behind is called **hydrolate**, an example is rose water. Oils from **citrus peel** are usually obtained by **cold pressing**.

Every oil has typical main components. In the oil of the **clove** it is **eugenol**, which is also used in dentistry. **Thymol** gives thyme oil its strongly **antiseptic**, that is germ-killing, effect. The oil of true chamomile is deep blue, because of the substance **chamazulene**. In eucalyptus oil, **1,8-cineole** is the main component by quantity.

Essential oils are used for perfumes, soaps, foods and in herbal medicine. But they are **very concentrated**. Undiluted, they can irritate the skin, and even small amounts can do harm if swallowed. Some oils such as peppermint or eucalyptus oil are dangerous for **small children**. They should therefore be used only diluted and according to instructions, and kept tightly closed.

gewusst: For one kilogram of rose oil, several tonnes of rose petals are needed.
The blue chamazulene is not yet present in the chamomile flowers themselves, it only forms during distillation.

teile.einleitung: Some plants produce seeds without fertilisation taking place. This phenomenon is called apomixis. The offspring are then usually exact copies, that is clones, of the mother plant.
wichtigste: **Apomixis** means seed formation without fertilisation.
Another technical term for it is **agamospermy**.
The **common dandelion** usually forms its seeds apomictically.
In **brambles** and **lady’s mantle**, many microspecies arose this way.
In **citrus fruits**, several seedlings often grow from one seed.
Many apomictic plants are **polyploid**.

abschnitte.text: Normally a seed forms when two reproductive cells fuse. In **apomixis** it is different: the embryo in the seed forms **without fertilisation**. That is why the offspring are usually **clones** of the mother plant. People also speak of **agamospermy**, which means seed formation without the fusion of reproductive cells. This must not be confused with **autogamy**, self-fertilisation.

A well-known example is the **common dandelion**. It usually forms its seeds without fertilisation. The plants in a meadow are therefore often clones. The **true brambles** (Rubus) also often form their seeds apomictically. This is why hundreds of **microspecies**, hard to tell apart, have been described in Europe. In the Alps, **lady’s mantle** (Alchemilla) is a classic example: most of its species reproduce in this way.

In many **citrus species**, extra seedlings grow from the tissue of the ovule. This is called **nucellar embryony**. Several little plants can thus sprout from a single seed. These are clones of the mother plant. Gardeners can use this to raise plants that are exactly like the mother.

Many apomicts are **polyploid**. This means they have more than two sets of chromosomes, for example triploid dandelions. In them the normal cell division for reproductive cells is often disturbed. Apomixis gets around this problem. For **plant breeding**, apomixis is very interesting: hybrid seed splits up again in the next generation. With apomixis, **hybrid varieties** could reproduce themselves true to type, and their good qualities would be kept.

gewusst: The term apomixis comes from Greek and means roughly “without mixing”.
Some grasses, for example some meadow-grasses, also form their seeds apomictically.

teile.einleitung: Species extinction means that animal and plant species disappear from the Earth for ever. Extinction has always happened in the history of the Earth, sometimes even in huge waves. Today, however, species are disappearing much faster than naturally, and humans are the main reason.
wichtigste: A species is extinct when not a single living thing of that species is left.
The background extinction rate is the natural rate of extinction without mass extinctions.
In the history of the Earth there have been five big mass extinctions.
The biggest was the Permian-Triassic event about 252 million years ago.
66 million years ago the dinosaurs disappeared, linked to the impact at Chicxulub.
According to the IPBES, the intergovernmental biodiversity panel, around 1 million species are threatened with extinction.
The main driver on land is the change in land use.

abschnitte.text: A species is **extinct** when its last living member has died, and it never comes back. Even without disasters, individual species die out again and again, and this is the **background extinction rate**. When very many species disappear in a short time, people speak of a **mass extinction**. Many researchers think that we are right now at the start of a sixth mass extinction.

In the last 500 million years there have been five big mass extinctions. The worst was the **Permian-Triassic event** about 252 million years ago, when most of all marine species died out, probably because of gigantic volcanic eruptions. 66 million years ago an asteroid struck at **Chicxulub** in Mexico. After that the dinosaurs died out, except for the ancestors of birds.

The flightless **dodo** lived on the island of Mauritius and was wiped out in the 17th century by sailors and introduced animals. The passenger pigeon was once the commonest bird in North America, with billions of birds. It disappeared through hunting, and the last passenger pigeon, called Martha, died in 1914 in a zoo. The mammoth also disappeared, probably partly because of human hunting.

In 2019 the **IPBES** examined the most important reasons. On land, the change in **land use** comes first, that is, the clearing of forests, the draining of moors and the building of roads and settlements. Other reasons are overfishing and hunting, climate change, pollution and **invasive species**. According to the report, around 1 million animal and plant species are threatened with extinction.

The International Union for Conservation of Nature, the **IUCN**, keeps the **Red List** of threatened species. It sorts species into categories, from not threatened to extinct. The category EW means extinct in the wild, and the species then lives only in zoos or gardens. Switzerland also has its own Red Lists for its animals and plants.

In Switzerland the bear, wolf, lynx, ibex and bearded vulture were wiped out in the past. Through protection and reintroduction, some have returned: the **ibex** was released again from 1911, and the bearded vulture has flown in the National Park again since 1991. The wolf came back by itself from Italy. Such successes show that protection measures can work.

begriffe.erklaerung: A time when very many species die out in a short time.
A list of threatened animal and plant species.
An introduced species that harms native species.
The intergovernmental biodiversity panel, which examines the state of nature.

gewusst: More than 99 per cent of all species that ever lived on Earth are extinct today.
Birds are the last living descendants of the dinosaurs.
The dodo was only described in more detail by Europeans around 1600, and had already disappeared about 100 years later.

teile.einleitung: Woodlice are small grey animals that you find under stones and flowerpots. Although they live on land, they are not insects but crustaceans. In the garden they are useful helpers, because they eat dead plant material.
wichtigste: Woodlice belong to the crustaceans.
An adult woodlouse has 14 legs.
You often find them under damp stones.
They eat mainly rotting plant material.
The pill woodlouse rolls itself into a ball when in danger.
A hard shell protects their body.

abschnitte.text: Woodlice belong to the **crustaceans**, so they are related to crabs and prawns. Most woodlouse species live in the sea, but some also live on land. An adult woodlouse has **14 legs**, which is seven pairs of legs. This sets it clearly apart from insects, which have six legs. Its body is flat and divided into many segments.

Land woodlice need **moisture**, or they dry out. That is why you find them **under damp stones**, under leaves, wood and flowerpots. During the day they hide, and at night they become active. The common woodlouse is called **Kellerassel** in German, which means cellar woodlouse, because you often find it **in damp cellars**. Common woodlice are mostly **grey**.

Woodlice eat mainly **rotting plant material** such as wilted leaves and rotten wood. In doing so they break up the material. Fungi and bacteria can then break it down further more easily. This produces fertile **humus**. In the compost heap, woodlice are therefore welcome helpers.

The woodlouse’s body is protected by a **hard shell**. Because it does not grow with the animal, the woodlouse has to **moult** as it grows. It sheds first the rear half and later the front half. The **pill woodlouse** has a special trick. When it feels threatened, it **rolls itself up into a ball**, so that only the shell can be seen.

gewusst: The females carry their eggs and the newly hatched young for a time in a brood pouch on the underside of the body.
Land woodlice breathe with modified gills and therefore need damp air.

teile.einleitung: Antarctica is the very cold continent at the South Pole. It is almost completely covered by a thick shell of ice and is nearly one and a half times as big as Europe. No people live here permanently, but penguins, seals and researchers from all over the world do.
wichtigste: Antarctica is the continent around the South Pole.
The Antarctic often means the whole region together with the surrounding sea.
Around 98 per cent of the area is covered by ice.
Most of the Earth’s fresh water is found here.
In 1983, minus 89.2 degrees was measured at Vostok station.
The Antarctic Treaty of 1959 protects the continent for peace and research.
Roald Amundsen was the first to reach the South Pole, in 1911.

abschnitte.text: At about 14 million square kilometres, **Antarctica** is the fifth-largest continent. Almost its whole area lies under an **ice sheet** that is on average around 2 kilometres thick. In some places the ice is over 4 kilometres thick. This ice holds about 70 per cent of the Earth’s fresh water.

Antarctica is the coldest, windiest and driest continent. At the Russian station **Vostok**, minus 89.2 degrees Celsius was measured in 1983. Because it hardly ever snows, Antarctica counts as the largest desert on Earth. In winter it is dark for months, and in summer the sun shines day and night.

On the coasts live **emperor penguins**, the largest penguins in the world, and Adélie penguins. Seals such as the leopard seal and the Weddell seal hunt in the icy sea. Whales come in summer to eat **krill**, tiny crustaceans that exist there in huge numbers. On the land itself only mosses, lichens and two species of flowering plants grow.

abschnitte.titel: The race to the South Pole
abschnitte.text: For a long time Antarctica was a blank spot on the map. The Norwegian **Roald Amundsen** reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911 as the first person ever. The Briton Robert Falcon Scott arrived a good month later and died with his companions on the way back. Their stories are among the best-known adventures in the history of exploration.

In the **Antarctic Treaty** of 1959, states agreed that Antarctica may only be used peacefully. The military and mining are forbidden, and research is at the centre. Around 70 research stations study climate, ice and animals there, and in summer several thousand people live on the continent. In old ice cores, researchers, including some from Switzerland, read what the climate was like hundreds of thousands of years ago.

The highest mountain in Antarctica is **Mount Vinson**, at almost 4,900 metres. Under the ice are hidden whole mountain ranges and over 400 lakes of liquid water. The largest of them is Lake Vostok, which lies under almost 4 kilometres of ice. If all the ice were to melt, sea level would rise by about 58 metres.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge mass of ice that covers a whole land.
Small crustaceans, the main food of many whales and penguins.
An agreement that protects Antarctica for peace and research.
A long cylinder of ice from the depths that contains old air and traces of the climate.

gewusst: Antarctica has no time zone of its own, each research station chooses its own time.
Although Antarctica is full of ice, less precipitation falls in its interior than in the Sahara.
In the icy winter, male emperor penguins incubate the egg on their feet for around two months.

teile.einleitung: The apricot is an orange, velvety stone fruit. In Switzerland it grows mainly in the Valais, where it is harvested in summer. In Austria it is called Marille.
wichtigste: The apricot is a stone fruit and belongs to the rose family.
Ripe apricots are orange and have velvety soft skin.
In Austria the apricot is called Marille.
Most Swiss apricots grow in the canton of Valais.
In the Valais the harvest is mainly in July and August.
The bitter kernels inside the stone can be poisonous and should not be eaten.

abschnitte.text: The apricot grows on a small tree from the **rose family**. Its fruit is roundish, orange and has **velvety soft skin**. Inside is a hard **stone**, which is why it counts as a **stone fruit**, like the cherry, plum and peach. The **peach** looks similar to it, but is usually bigger. The flesh is sweet and slightly sour.

The apricot originally comes from Asia and reached Europe along long trade routes. Its scientific name is **Prunus armeniaca**, because people used to believe it came from Armenia. In the German-speaking world it has different names. In Austria and parts of southern Germany people say **Marille**. In Switzerland and Germany the name Aprikose is usual.

The canton of **Valais** is the most important growing area in Switzerland. In the Rhône valley it is sunny, dry and warm in summer, which the trees like. The harvest takes place mainly in **July and August**. A well-known traditional Valais variety is called **Luizet**. One problem is spring: apricot trees **blossom very early**, and a cold night can freeze the blossoms. Farmers then sometimes protect them from the frost with water or fire.

Apricots are eaten fresh, dried or as **jam**. Well known are apricot tart and Marillenknödel (apricot dumplings).
